Close, friend, but the text goes further than that. These disciples tell Paul, “we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” (Acts 19:2) They haven't heard of Him at all, which is a lot more than not knowing Him well. Then Paul asks, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” (Acts 19:3)

Yes, friend. “On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.” (Acts 19:5) Paul explains, and they listen. They hear that John told people to believe in Jesus, and then they are baptized.

The text says the opposite, friend. “On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.” (Acts 19:5) Once Paul explains about John and Jesus, these disciples go ahead and are baptized. The passage doesn't show any holding back.

explanations.answer: The Holy Spirit comes on them and they speak in tongues and prophesy
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, friend. “…the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.” (Acts 19:6) It all happens right after Paul lays his hands on them. Plain and powerful, with no extra details needed.

explanations.answer: A bright light flashes around them and they all fall to the ground
explanations.explanation: No flash of light shows up in this scene, friend. The text says, “…the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.” (Acts 19:6) Nobody is described falling down.

explanations.answer: The whole building shakes and every door in the place flies open
explanations.explanation: That's a big scene, friend, but it isn't this one. In Ephesus the text says, “…the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.” (Acts 19:6) Nothing about shaking walls or flying doors is mentioned. The text keeps its focus on the men and what happens to them.

Not this time, friend. After the three months, “…some of them stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way…” (Acts 19:9) So not every single person believed. Paul still spoke boldly for those three months.

That's right, friend. Some of them “…stubbornly refused to believe and publicly maligned the Way…” (Acts 19:9) Three months of bold, persuasive talk didn't win over everyone in the room. Even so, Paul didn't quit. He just moved the conversation to a new place.

explanations.answer: Takes his disciples to the lecture hall of Tyrannus
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul “…took his disciples and left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.” (Acts 19:9) He changes the location and keeps going. When one door closes, he finds the next one.

explanations.answer: Sails out of Ephesus and heads back to Syria
explanations.explanation: Paul isn't packing a bag, friend. He leaves the synagogue, but he stays in Ephesus, where he conducts daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus (Acts 19:9). That goes on for two years (Acts 19:10). Nobody in this scene boards a boat.

explanations.answer: Stays and argues in that same synagogue every day
explanations.explanation: Almost, friend, but Paul changes rooms. The text says he “…left the synagogue to conduct daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.” (Acts 19:9) The daily talks are real, but they happen in a different place. He took his disciples with him.

explanations.answer: Everyone in the province of Asia
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says “…everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.” (Acts 19:10) That's a whole province, from one lecture hall and two years of daily discussions. The word got a lot farther than that one room.

explanations.answer: Only the people living in Ephesus
explanations.explanation: The text says it reached further than that, friend. “…everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.” (Acts 19:10) Ephesus is where Paul is, but the whole province is where the word lands. Think of a batch that gets passed down the whole street.

explanations.answer: Only the disciples Paul brought along
explanations.explanation: It went way past that little group, friend. The text says “…everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.” (Acts 19:10) Paul's disciples were with him, but they weren't the only ones listening. Two years of daily discussions covered a lot of ground.

explanations.answer: Handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. “…even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick…” (Acts 19:12) The text says God did these extraordinary miracles through Paul's hands. Everyday cloth, and God did something extraordinary with it.

explanations.answer: Water from the pool of Siloam
explanations.explanation: Water from the pool of Siloam doesn't come up in this scene, friend. Here the text says, “…even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick…” (Acts 19:12) It's cloth that gets carried.

explanations.answer: Oil that Paul had prayed over
explanations.explanation: No oil appears in this scene, friend. The text says, “…even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick…” (Acts 19:12) The things that were carried are cloth. Same cloth, new job.

The text says there's more, friend. When the cloth reached the sick, “…the diseases and evil spirits left them.” (Acts 19:12) That's diseases and evil spirits, both. Don't let half the list slip past you.
Yes, friend. The text says “…the diseases and evil spirits left them.” (Acts 19:12) Both left, so it wasn't only the diseases. That's a full list, and God did all of it through Paul's hands.
That's the name, friend. The exorcists said, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” (Acts 19:13) They pointed to Paul's preaching as their line. I think that's about to cause trouble.
Peter doesn't get named in these exorcists' line, friend. They said, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” (Acts 19:13) Paul is the one they point to. Peter isn't part of this line.

Barnabas was a companion of Paul (Acts 13:2), but he isn't the name in this line, friend. The exorcists said, “I command you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims.” (Acts 19:13) Paul is the one in Ephesus whose preaching they're borrowing. Barnabas isn't part of this scene.

explanations.answer: It knows Jesus and knows about Paul but asks who they are
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what it says, friend. “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” (Acts 19:15) The sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, get a question aimed right at them. It's a question nobody wants to get at work, let alone from that.

explanations.answer: It will only leave if Paul comes and tells it himself
explanations.explanation: The spirit never asks for Paul, friend. What it says is, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” (Acts 19:15) It mentions Paul, then turns to the sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest's sons, with a question.

explanations.answer: It has never once heard anyone use the name of Jesus
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around, friend. The spirit says, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” (Acts 19:15) It says it knows Jesus. Then it asks who the sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest's sons, are.

explanations.answer: They run out naked and wounded
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, friend. “The attack was so violent that they ran out of the house naked and wounded.” (Acts 19:16) The seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, are the ones who leave this way. This is a heavy part, and I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: They are carried out in chains
explanations.explanation: Nobody is chained in this scene, friend. The text says, “…they ran out of the house naked and wounded.” (Acts 19:16) They get out on their own two feet. It's a hard moment, so let's keep the details straight.

explanations.answer: They are led out blind by the hand
explanations.explanation: That one isn't in the text, friend. The passage says, “…they ran out of the house naked and wounded.” (Acts 19:16) Nobody is led by the hand, and nobody is called blind. It's a heavy moment, and the text keeps it short.

That's right, friend. “…fear came over all of them. So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.” (Acts 19:17) The news reached the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus. After it, they treated His name with great respect.

The text says it plainly, friend. After the news spread, “…fear came over all of them. So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.” (Acts 19:17) The name of Jesus is held in high honor, not set aside. Everyone in Ephesus, Jews and Greeks, took notice.

Yes, friend. “Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds.” (Acts 19:18) These are people who had already believed, and they come forward anyway. They disclosed their deeds. That takes guts, and I'd rather confess a burnt batch.

explanations.answer: Ask to be baptized a second time
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. “Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds.” (Acts 19:18) Baptism isn't mentioned in this part. These believers come forward to confess.

No collection is taken up here, friend. The text says, “Many who had believed now came forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds.” (Acts 19:18) It's about what they did, and they say it out loud. Gifts for the poor aren't part of this scene.

explanations.answer: Burn them in front of everyone
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. “…a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books and burned them in front of everyone.” (Acts 19:19) When the value of those books was calculated, it came to fifty thousand drachmas. And they still lit the match in front of everyone.

No shovels in this scene, friend. The text says they “…brought their books and burned them in front of everyone.” (Acts 19:19) They burned them, and they did it in front of everyone.
